faults.fault: Figure shows the tail boom extended; hub-to-tail ~510 mm by the 100 mm scale bar (rotor radius measures ~205 mm, consistent), exceeding 450 mm, while text claims a folded 380 mm stack. Folding the tail beside the nacelle would cut its yaw moment arm, and that is not checked.

faults.fault: The spring pad/caliper is drawn on a horizontal yaw disc, not the rotor shaft, so as drawn it locks yaw, not the rotor; text never says what the pad acts on or its holding torque.

Stop simulation uses aero torque at 11 m/s only. With fixed pitch, a 22 m/s gust trips the latch; my estimate of phase-short torque (Ke 0.0298, 0.25 ohm) balances the aero torque near ~100 rad/s (~30% of top speed), so staying below 10% depends on the unspecified pad.
Inertia 0.0016 used for stored energy (87.1 J) but 0.0012 in the stop simulation (65 J); '79.2 J matched to 87.1 J' is not a real check. The stop time would still be a few seconds.
39.6 A peak short against an IRLZ44N 47 A rating that applies at 25 C case: thin margin.
Step panels go 1, 3, 4 (step 2 missing); slip ring is drawn at the post base with an external cable that would twist with yaw.

C1.why: Power and survival are computed (30.7 W, 15.2 MPa), but cube fit conflicts with the picture and staying parked at high wind is unverified.

C2.why: Phase-short braking works in the operating range; holding with a fixed-pitch rotor in strong wind relies on an unspecified pad.

C3.why: Most numbers re-derive exactly (102 W, 0.109 N m, 15.2 MPa, 0.367 mm, 2.97 mm), but the stop/hold claim is unsupported at high wind and the inertia is inconsistent.

C4.why: Shows rotor, generator cutaway, tail, slip ring and brake, but the tail is unfolded beyond the cube and the brake sits on the yaw disc.

C5.why: Plain, buildable parts and honest component ratings; risks are short.

C6.why: Understandable but jargon-heavy; brake action not explained.

C8.why: Generally clean render, but brake placement and the skipped step number are errors.

b3.better_why: B's collective feathering plus generator short handles both the 22 m/s survival and the stop-and-stay requirement robustly, and its numbers check out; its main defect is a four-blade picture. C is numerically careful but its fixed-pitch rotor cannot be shown to stay parked in strong wind, and its picture breaks the cube. A contradicts itself (fixed pitch that must feather).

faults.fault: Modal mass of 20 t and 0.4% damping are assumed with no deck-mass basis, and there is no modal test before off-site fabrication of a tuned device.
The 500 kg mass hangs on two springs and two dashpots with no guides; rocking and pendulum sway are not addressed.
The cover tray with the '+/-50 mm stops' hangs from rods off the moving mass, so the stops move with it and cannot limit stroke; stops are not in the text.
Mass block ~1.3 m long by the 500 mm scale bar, about 3x the volume of 500 kg of steel; step panels use differing human scales.
Damping ratio given as both 0.0933 and 0.0956; 'spring compression' while the picture shows hanging springs; Risks section empty.

C1.why: Uses the span and 1.9 Hz correctly and keeps the deck look, but the comfort level is not shown to be met.

C3.why: Tuning, stiffness, damping and sag re-derive exactly, but the off-peak response and unsupported crowd model mislead the comfort result.

03.better_why: Both are sound midspan TMDs. B measures the bridge first, uses a larger guided twin mass with a stated comfort target, and its numbers are conservative. A computes carefully but evaluates the response off-peak, leans on an unsupported crowd model and assumed modal mass, and lists no risks. A's picture is more faithful.
